title: A Visitor for the Bell
premise: Mirabel Hartwell is hired to survey Hollow Bell House, a crumbling estate whose measurements refuse to stay true — rooms gain feet overnight, and the house seems to appraise her back. On the porch she finds Wren, the imaginary friend of her childhood, unchanged after twenty years, and he is not hers alone: he belongs to the house, summoned by founders who bound a dying child's love into a ritual that keeps something fed beneath the bell tower. As Mirabel's memories surface, she learns she was meant to be the offering and escaped once before; now Wren must either complete the founders' ritual or break it. In the end Mirabel chooses to stand in the circle herself, offering love instead of duty, and Wren — given the choice between finishing the ritual and saving her — shatters the bell, unmaking the house and himself, leaving Mirabel alive with a porch that holds only morning light.
about_author: Tamsin Halloran is a former architectural conservator from coastal Maine who spent a decade documenting houses too damaged to save. Her fiction explores what buildings remember when no one will live in them honestly.

chapters.title: The Measurement Problem
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She arrives at Hollow Bell House to begin a court-ordered appraisal, but her laser measure returns impossible numbers — a hallway longer inside than out. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into the first real fear.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Following her own ritual of counting doors and leaving lights on, she surveys the ground floor and finds one door more at dusk than at dawn. The beat is the comfort of routine failing as protection.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. At dawn a figure waits on the porch steps: Wren, her childhood imaginary friend, exactly as she left him at age nine. Joy and terror arrive together; he says simply, 'You came back. It waited.'

chapters.title: What Wren Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Inside the house's walls-between-walls, Wren recalls being made — stitched from a lonely girl's need by founders who wanted a keeper for the thing under the bell. He loves Mirabel and knows he was built to deliver her. The beat is guilt wearing devotion's face.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. In the library she finds the Hartwell family ledger: her ancestors founded the house, and every third generation 'a visitor for the bell.' Her grandmother's name is crossed out; hers is written in fresh ink. Dread becomes inheritance.

chapters.title: Rooms That Grow
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Overnight the east wing has added a nursery that appears on no blueprint, wallpapered in patterns from her childhood bedroom. The house is furnishing itself around her memories. The beat is violation through intimacy.

chapters.title: Wren's Warning
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren urges Mirabel to leave before the new moon, refusing to explain, while the house punishes his disobedience — doors seal, lights die room by room. The beat is love against duty beginning its argument.

chapters.title: The Bell Tower
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She climbs the tower and finds the great bronze bell, cracked but humming, and beneath it a stone basin stained dark. Something far below shifts when her shadow crosses the rail. The beat is awe tipping into horror.

chapters.title: Neighbor Knowledge
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. In town, an elderly archivist recognizes the house's name and goes white: her own sister 'visited' in 1961. She gives Mirabel a photograph of the founding family — and Mirabel sees herself in it, aged nine. The beat is the past confirming the trap.

chapters.title: Memory Unlocked
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Triggered by the photo, Mirabel remembers: at nine she was brought here as the offering, and Wren — her creation, her protector — hid her from the founders and got her out. She never imagined him away; she left him behind on purpose. Grief and gratitude collide.

chapters.title: The Ritual, Explained
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren confesses everything: the founders bound a starving presence under the bell, fed by a willing heart every sixty years. If the debt goes unpaid at this new moon, it takes the whole valley. He must finish the ritual — with her. The beat is duty's terrible arithmetic.

chapters.title: Running Out of House
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Mirabel tries to flee; the house rearranges, returning her to the nursery no matter which door she takes. Wren opens a window onto open air three stories up and begs her to jump to him. Trust is tested mid-air. The beat is desperate faith.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The house speaks through Wren briefly — the founders' voices layered over his own — revealing they never intended sacrifice; they intended a hostage kept loving until she'd walk in willingly. Wren retches afterward. The beat is complicity and rage.

chapters.title: A Third Option
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Studying the ledger's margins, Mirabel finds her grandmother's hidden notes: the binding can be broken if the bell is rung backward by someone the house loves freely — a crack in the founders' design. Hope, fragile and specific.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Debt
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The old archivist arrives at the gate at dusk, drawn by the same pull that took her sister, and Mirabel must bar the door against her. The beat is watching duty devour a stranger, and knowing her turn approaches.

chapters.title: New Moon Eve
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The house begins its preparations: candles lighting themselves, the basin filling, the nursery door standing open like an invitation. Wren sharpens a length of iron rebar into a tool that is either a key or a weapon. The beat is grim readiness.

chapters.title: The Circle
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The house takes Mirabel in her sleep and sets her in the tower circle, robed, the founders' words moving her mouth. Wren breaks the trance by speaking their private childhood word — proof he is hers, not theirs. The beat is love cutting through enchantment.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren stands in the circle holding the iron, ordered by the house to finish the ritual, offered Mirabel's life as the price of his obedience. He chooses: he strikes the bell backward instead. The beat is the book's moral climax — devotion refusing its designed purpose.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings Backward
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The reversed toll unmakes the binding; the thing below rises furious through the collapsing floors, and Mirabel and Wren flee down a staircase that is eating itself. The beat is pure velocity, the house screaming in architecture.

chapters.title: What Wren Is For
chapters.summary: POV Wren. At the threshold the unbound presence seizes Wren — he was made of the house, and it can take him back. To hold the door open for Mirabel, he lets it. His last words are the childhood word. The beat is sacrifice as the truest form of the love he was built from.

chapters.title: Morning Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Dawn: Hollow Bell House stands gutted and silent, the bell split down the middle, the basin dry. Mirabel files her final report — structure unsound, recommend demolition — and leaves the porch light burning anyway. The beat is grief with a floor under it.

chapters.title: A Visitor, After All
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel, coda. Months later, in her city apartment, the doorbell rings. On the mat: a pressed sprig of wisteria from the house's trellis, and faintly, in a child's handwriting, the private word. She smiles through tears and leaves the door unlocked. The beat is love outlasting its architecture.
